opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it is that the people using the agent are generating the most valuable signal we could possibly get, because they're showing us what real tasks on the real web actually look like, as opposed to what we imagined they'd look like when we built our initial benchmarks.

There are a few layers to it. The most direct one is just outcomes: did the agent complete what the person asked for, did they have to step in, did they abandon the task halfway through? Those interventions are incredibly informative. When someone takes over and clicks the right button themselves, that's essentially a demonstration of what the agent should have done at that step, and we can turn those moments into training data.

The second layer is understanding the distribution of tasks. Early on, you have a hypothesis about what people will want, maybe booking things, comparing products, filling out forms. Then you watch actual usage and discover all these long-tail workflows and weird site designs you never would have prioritized. That reshapes what we collect data on and what we evaluate against, so the training mix starts to mirror what people actually need rather than what's easy to measure.

And then there's a preference piece. Even when the agent technically succeeds, people have opinions about how it went. Did it check in at the right moments? Did it ask too many questions, or too few? Did it take a sensible path or wander around the site? That kind of feedback is more subtle, but it's really important for making the agent feel trustworthy rather than just functional.

Of course, all of this has to be done carefully. People are browsing on their own accounts, sometimes with personal information on the page, so we're thoughtful about consent, about what we retain, and about stripping out anything sensitive before it ever gets near training. But done right, it creates this loop where the more people use it, the better it gets at exactly the things they care about, and that's the flywheel we're really excited about.

r001.rationale: The response says observing actual usage reveals long-tail workflows and reshapes data collection so the training mix reflects what people need.

r002.rationale: The response discusses varied workflows and site designs, but does not state that development avoids prioritizing websites and progressively expanding that list.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've thought about a lot, because the obvious thing to do with a web navigation agent is to just go collect a big static dataset of demonstrations, train on it, and ship it. And that gets you something, but it doesn't really reflect how people actually use the web, and it goes stale fast. Websites change, the tasks people care about change.

So the way we think about it is that user activity is the richest signal we have, and we want it to shape the model at a few different levels. The first is just what tasks we care about at all. When people use the product, we see the kinds of things they ask for, which sites they go to, where they get stuck. That tells us where to focus data collection and evaluation, rather than guessing from the outside.

The second level is implicit feedback. When an agent takes an action and the user corrects it, or takes over and does the step themselves, or abandons the task entirely, that's a very strong signal about where the model is failing. We don't necessarily need someone to sit down and label that. The trajectory itself tells you the agent did something the user didn't want. And conversely, when a task runs end to end and the user accepts the result, that's a positive example of a successful trajectory on a real website, which is much more valuable than a synthetic one.

The third piece, and the one I'm probably most careful about, is turning that into training signal responsibly. You can't just scoop up everyone's browsing and throw it into a training set. A lot of this is personal, it involves logged-in sessions, financial pages, health information. So we think hard about what gets opted into, what gets aggregated, what gets anonymized, and what never leaves the user's context at all. For a lot of it, the right move is to learn from the structure of the interaction, the fact that the user intervened at a particular step on a particular kind of page, rather than from the specific content.

And then the loop closes with evaluation. User activity doesn't just shape what goes into training, it shapes how we measure. If we see that people are increasingly trying to use the agent for, say, multi-step booking flows, then our evals need to reflect that, or we'll be optimizing for a benchmark that no one cares about anymore.

So the short version is that we treat the deployed system as part of the research process. The users are, in a sense, defining the distribution for us, and our job is to listen carefully, learn from it in a way that respects them, and feed it back in a tight enough loop that the model keeps improving on the things people actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says observed user requests and behavior determine which tasks receive focus in data collection, so user activity guides task types in post-training data.

r002.rationale: The response describes using user activity to guide development, but does not state that development avoids prioritizing websites and expanding that list over time.

astra-6.text:
One way is to learn from demonstrations. As a user goes through a task on a website, the sequence of actions they take—what they click on, what they type, and how they move between pages—can become a training example. The model learns to map the user’s goal and the current state of the page to the next action.

But activity alone doesn’t necessarily tell you what was correct. People explore, make mistakes, and backtrack. So you want to connect those actions to whether the task was actually completed, and use corrections or explicit feedback where you have it. That gives you a way to improve the model from real use without treating every click as something it should imitate.

r001.rationale: The response says user action sequences can become training examples, but does not state that observed activity guides which task types are included in post-training data.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to do that is to learn from demonstrations. As a user performs a task in the browser, you can capture the sequence of actions they take—what they click on, what they type, and how the page changes—and use that as supervision for the model. The model learns to map the user’s instruction and the current state of the page to the next action.

But user activity isn’t automatically a perfect training signal. People make mistakes, backtrack, or take different paths to accomplish the same thing. So you want to account for that and, where possible, use feedback about whether the task was actually completed successfully. Corrections are particularly useful: when the model gets something wrong and the user intervenes, that gives you an example of where its behavior needs to improve.
